questions.q: State the condition for forward biasing a p-n junction diode and name the majority carriers that cross the junction in this condition.
questions.a: Forward bias: p-side connected to positive terminal of battery, n-side to negative terminal. Majority carriers crossing: holes from p-side diffuse to n-side, electrons from n-side diffuse to p-side. A wrong answer (e.g., "n-side to positive") reveals confusion about which polarity reduces the barrier; the student likely memorized the diagram without understanding that the applied field must oppose the built-in field.

questions.q: Explain why the depletion layer width decreases under forward bias and increases under reverse bias, referencing the direction of the applied electric field relative to the built-in field.
questions.a: Under forward bias, the applied field (positive to negative from p to n) opposes the built-in field (n to p), reducing net field strength; fewer uncovered ions are needed to balance the reduced field, so depletion width shrinks. Under reverse bias, applied field reinforces built-in field, requiring more uncovered charge → wider depletion region. A wrong answer (e.g., "forward bias widens depletion layer") shows the student confuses the effect of applied voltage on the space-charge region.

questions.q: A silicon diode's forward V-I curve gives: at I = 10 mA, V = 0.70 V; at I = 20 mA, V = 0.80 V. Calculate the dynamic resistance r_d in this region. Show unit tracking.
questions.a: r_d = ΔV/ΔI = (0.80 V – 0.70 V) / (20 mA – 10 mA) = 0.10 V / 10 mA = 0.10 V / 0.010 A = 10 Ω. Unit check: V/A = Ω. A wrong answer (e.g., 100 Ω) typically comes from forgetting to convert mA to A (0.10 V / 10 mA = 0.01 Ω if mA treated as A) or misreading the graph points.

questions.q: Compare the physical origin of forward current and reverse saturation current in a p-n junction diode. Why is reverse current nearly voltage-independent until breakdown?
questions.a: Forward current: diffusion of injected minority carriers (electrons in p-side, holes in n-side) due to lowered barrier; exponential with voltage. Reverse saturation current: drift of thermally generated minority carriers (electrons in p-side, holes in n-side) across the junction; limited by minority carrier concentration, not by barrier height, so nearly constant with reverse voltage. A wrong answer (e.g., "reverse current is due to majority carriers") indicates misunderstanding of which carriers are available on each side under reverse bias.

questions.q: A student claims: "In reverse bias, the diode current is zero because the barrier becomes infinite." Evaluate this statement and correct it.
questions.a: The statement is false. Reverse bias increases barrier height to (V_0 + V), but it never becomes infinite; a small drift current (µA) flows due to thermally generated minority carriers being swept across the junction. This reverse saturation current is non-zero and nearly constant until breakdown. The student's error: confusing "very high resistance" with "infinite resistance" and ignoring minority carrier generation.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a 9 V battery, a 1 kΩ resistor, a silicon diode, and a multimeter to verify that the diode conducts in only one direction. Specify the measurements you would take and the expected observations.
questions.a: Connect battery, resistor, and diode in series. Set multimeter to 200 mA DC range. Measure current with diode in forward bias (p to battery +): expect ~2–5 mA (limited by resistor). Reverse diode connections: expect reading ~0 µA (multimeter may show 0.00 mA). Swap multimeter to µA range for reverse: expect < 1 µA. A poor answer (e.g., "measure voltage across diode only") fails to demonstrate the rectifying action via current measurement.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A p-n junction diode is a two-terminal ______ device formed by joining p-type and n-type materials with metallic contacts; under forward bias (p-side connected to positive terminal, n-side to negative), the applied voltage opposes the built-in potential barrier, narrowing the depletion region and allowing majority carriers to diffuse across the junction, producing a current in milliamperes; under reverse bias (polarity reversed), the applied voltage reinforces the barrier, widening the depletion region and permitting only a tiny drift current of minority carriers (microamperes) until breakdown voltage is reached.
Fill in the blank: Observe a ______ LED torch: when you flip the switch, the LED lights up instantly; if you accidentally insert the batteries backward, it stays dark.
Fill in the blank: Slowly increase voltage with p-side to positive (forward bias) and record I vs V; notice current remains negligible until ~______ V, then rises sharply.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can: (1) draw and label the circuit diagrams for forward and reverse bias, showing correct battery polarity and current direction; (2) explain how depletion layer width and barrier potential change with bias using band diagrams; (3) calculate dynamic resistance r_d = ΔV/ΔI from a given V-I characteristic curve; (4) distinguish.
